scenes.title: Isolation Levels
scenes.narration: Isolation levels let you dial how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's uncommitted or in-flight work, trading strictness against throughput.

scenes.title: The concurrency phenomena
bullets: Dirty read: you read another transaction's uncommitted change that may be rolled back
Non-repeatable read: a row you read changes if you read it again in the same transaction
Phantom read: a re-run query returns new rows inserted by another transaction
scenes.narration: Isolation levels exist to prevent three anomalies. A dirty read happens when you see changes another transaction has not yet committed, which may vanish on rollback. A non-repeatable read is when a row you already read has a different value if you read it again. A phantom read is when re-running the same query returns extra rows that another transaction inserted in between.

scenes.title: Levels versus phenomena prevented

left.title: Weaker isolation
points: READ UNCOMMITTED: allows dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads
READ COMMITTED: prevents dirty reads only
More concurrency, less locking, more anomalies

right.title: Stronger isolation
points: REPEATABLE READ: also prevents non-repeatable reads
SERIALIZABLE: prevents all three, including phantoms
Fewer anomalies, more locking, less concurrency

scenes.narration: The standard defines four levels along a spectrum. On the weaker end, READ UNCOMMITTED permits every anomaly, and READ COMMITTED blocks only dirty reads. On the stronger end, REPEATABLE READ also stops non-repeatable reads, and SERIALIZABLE stops phantoms too, making transactions behave as if run one after another. The tradeoff is clear: stronger isolation means more locking and less concurrency.

scenes.title: Setting the isolation level
scenes.narration: You choose an isolation level per transaction with SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL. Here we request REPEATABLE READ. Inside the transaction we read account one's balance twice. Because of the level we chose, no other transaction can change that row's value in between, so both reads return the same number. Raising the level to serializable would additionally protect us from phantom rows appearing.

scenes.title: Choosing a level
steps: Start with the database default, often READ COMMITTED
Raise to REPEATABLE READ when you re-read the same rows and need stability
Use SERIALIZABLE for logic that must be provably correct under concurrency
Expect more contention and retries as you raise the level
scenes.narration: Pick a level to match your needs. Most systems default to READ COMMITTED, which is a sensible baseline. Move to REPEATABLE READ when a transaction reads the same data more than once and needs it to stay stable. Reach for SERIALIZABLE only when correctness under heavy concurrency is non-negotiable, and be ready for more contention and serialization failures that you must retry.

scenes.text: Use the lowest isolation level that keeps your logic correct. Higher isolation buys safety with locking and reduced throughput, so only pay for what you need.
scenes.narration: The guiding principle is to use the lowest isolation level that still keeps your logic correct, because higher levels buy safety at the cost of locking and throughput.
